newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe shares seen on a firm course into 1997.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe shares seen on a firm course into 1997.

text.p: Zimbabwe's share market looks set to stay on a firm course into the new year on investor expectations that reasonable rains will boost the southern African country's agricultural-powered economy, share analysts said on Tuesday.

But they said the Zimbabwe Stock Exchange (ZSE) may also swing wildly on some days in reaction to a host of factors, including temporary spikes in inflation and speculation over talks between the government and international donors on a new aid programme.
Savvas Kyriakides, managing director of economic and share market analysts Dataworld, said volatile trade seen on the ZSE in the past fortnight after a two-month bull run was part of the wild swings.
The ZSE's main 57-counter industrial index has climbed back to around 7,000 over the days after plunging by over 400 points in the last two weeks from a record high of 7,167.55 on September.

"Although volatility can be expected, the general trend into early next year should be upwards assuming reasonable rains and the successful launch of ZIMPREST (Zimbabwe Programme for Economic and Social Transformation)," Kyriakides said.

President Robert Mugabe's government plans to launch the five-year ZIMPREST before the end of 1996, but still has to secure crucial funding from its main Western donors, including the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Local economists expect Zimbabwe's economy to grow by over five percent in 1997 for the second successive year if the country gets near-normal rains in the November-April farming season.
"Good rains will continue to be a good peg for some shares, with reasonable rains providing a solid investment base," Kyriakides told Reuters.

Leading Zimbabwean stock brokers Edwards and Company also believes the local bourse would continue to gain from falling interest rates -- quoted around 20 percent in the past month on the local money market from an average 24 percent in January.
"Bank lending rates are likely to drop further on the back of the fall in inflation in August to a three-year low of 17.7 percent," the company said in a commentary.
"Although inflation is expected to rise in the short-term, pressure is mounting on local (commercial) banks to reduce their lending rates from the current level of 30 percent.

"The continuing fall in (money) market rates has lowered the marginal cost of funds to financial institutions which, when passed on, will provide a welcome boost to the economy which is showing signs of recovery, primarily in the agricultural sector," it said.
